I am 63 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou my whole life. The land here on the North China Plain is good black soil, but it is tired after so many years, so I do not try anything fancy. I will stick to the wheat–maize rotation that my father taught me and that every household in the village still follows. My eight mu are already sown to winter wheat — I put in Jimai 22, an improved variety that the seed dealer at the township market has been selling for years and that gives stable yields. I will rotary-till before the next wheat sowing in autumn, but for the summer maize I will plant directly into the wheat stubble without tilling; that is how everyone here does it now, and it saves diesel and time during the busy harvest season. For fertilizer, the soil test van that comes to the village every spring says my nitrogen is low, so I spread about 100 jin of compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea or ammonium bicarbonate at green-up and heading — altogether about 18 kg of pure nitrogen per mu for the wheat. The maize gets less because the wheat stubble still has some fertility; I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and that is usually enough, about 12 kg nitrogen per mu. Wheat needs water at green-up, jointing, heading and grain-filling, so I will irrigate four times from the well. Maize is tougher — two good irrigations, one at the six-leaf stage and one at tasseling, are enough if the summer rains cooperate. Pests and weeds are a constant headache, so I spray insecticide twice and apply herbicide once for each crop; the wheat also needs a fungicide spray against powdery mildew because the humidity in May gets high. I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat and 550 kg per mu from the maize if the weather holds. That is the plan — nothing new, just steady work.
